Task T1: What does multiplying a graph mean?

0. Input and Code

Input is HW8_graph_data.json exported by the course notebook: the base mini-web (12 vertices, 23 weighted edges) and cluster_graph(n, seed=8) for n = 64, 128, 256, 512. Node order is the notebook's order, so row i and column i are node i. Rows are sources, columns are destinations. The weights are ignored in T1: A[i][j] = 1 exactly when the edge i → j exists.

All algorithms are my own Rust code: matrix products, Warshall, Boolean repeated squaring, BFS and SCC grouping are in src/lib.rs, the experiment is src/bin/T1.rs and the figures are drawn with the plotters crate (src/draw.rs). Python is used only for checking: hw8_check.py imports the course helpers, runs check_closure on every closure, compares A², A³ with NumPy and the SCCs with NetworkX, and times two NumPy versions as a reference.

1. A² and A³ Count Walks

In the ordinary integer product, (A·A)[i][j] = Σk A[i][k]·A[k][j] adds 1 for every middle vertex k with edges i → k → j, so A²[i][j] is the number of walks of length 2 from i to j, and by the same argument A³[i][j] is the number of walks of length 3. The products are computed with 64-bit integers.

Three-hop check, 0 Home → 4 Graphs

All walks 0 → a → b → 4 were listed by checking every pair (a, b) with edges 0 → a, a → b, b → 4:

#WalkPagesSimple path?
1[0, 1, 2, 4]0 Home → 1 Courses → 2 Algorithms → 4 Graphsyes
2[0, 1, 3, 4]0 Home → 1 Courses → 3 Trees → 4 Graphsyes

2 walks were found and A³[0][4] = 2, so the count matches the matrix entry. Here both walks happen to be simple paths. That is not true in general: for 1 Courses → 4 Graphs, A³[1][4] = 3 and one of the three walks goes around the cycle 1 ⇄ 4:

WalkPagesSimple path?
[1, 2, 3, 4]1 Courses → 2 Algorithms → 3 Trees → 4 Graphsyes
[1, 3, 2, 4]1 Courses → 3 Trees → 2 Algorithms → 4 Graphsyes
[1, 4, 1, 4]1 Courses → 4 Graphs → 1 Courses → 4 Graphsno (revisits 1, 4)

So matrix powers count walks, which may repeat vertices and edges, not simple paths.

2. Reflexive Transitive Closure, Two Ways

R[i][j] is true when j can be reached from i by a path of length 0 or more, so the diagonal is always true. Both methods start from I ∨ A and use only OR/AND, never unbounded walk counts:

  • Warshall: for k = 0 … n−1, for every i with R[i][k] true, set row i to row i OR row k. After step k, R[i][j] says whether there is a path whose intermediate vertices are all in {0, …, k}. One pass over all k gives the closure.
  • Repeated squaring: R ← R ⊙ R with the Boolean product (R ⊙ R)[i][j] = ORk (R[i][k] AND R[k][j]). If R covers paths of length ≤ L, the square covers ≤ 2L, so after s squarings all paths of length ≤ 2s are included. The loop stops when a squaring does not change the matrix; that last squaring is counted.

On the mini-web the longest shortest path is 5 edges (1 Courses → 4 → 5 → 6 → 8 → 11 Exit). Squaring covers lengths 2, 4, 8, so it changes the matrix three times and the fourth squaring confirms: 4 squarings. Each method was implemented twice in Rust: with bit rows (one u64 holds 64 entries) and with plain bool entries. All four results are identical, equal the BFS reachability from every vertex, and have a true diagonal.

The closure has 89 true entries out of 144. Its block shape already shows the structure: Home reaches everything, the "course" pages 1–4 reach the research part 5–8, the research part reaches the partners and Exit, but nothing goes back. 9 and 10 reach only each other, and Exit reaches only itself.

true / count added at this step selected cell (click any cell)

The widget recomputes the same matrices in JavaScript for the mini-web. Walks: choose k and click a cell to list the walks it counts. Warshall: each step allows one more intermediate vertex; orange cells are new. Repeated squaring: each step doubles the covered path length; the last step changes nothing and stops the loop.

3. Why One Multiplication or Checking Aⁿ > 0 Is Not Enough

  • One product (I ∨ A)² only covers paths of length ≤ 2. On the mini-web it has 58 true entries instead of 89; for example 0 Home → 6 Projects (length 2) is found, but 0 Home → 11 Exit (length 4) is not. A path may need up to n − 1 edges, so the products must be repeated.
  • Aⁿ > 0 asks for walks of exactly n steps, not "at most n". With n = 12 the Boolean A¹² has 85 true entries and misses (0, 0), (9, 10), (10, 9), (11, 11). (0, 0) and (11, 11) are missed because Home and Exit lie on no cycle, so no walk returns to them (reflexivity needs I). (9, 10) and (10, 9) are missed because the only way between Partner A and Partner B is the 2-cycle, so every walk between them has odd length and none has length 12. The closure needs I ∨ A ∨ A² ∨ … ∨ Aⁿ⁻¹, which is what (I ∨ A)2s gives.
  • Integer counts grow. If ordinary multiplication is used instead of OR/AND, the numbers of walks grow exponentially with the length, so a uint8 accumulator overflows (256 becomes 0, which would wrongly mean "unreachable"). Thresholding to 0/1 after every product, as the Boolean product does, avoids this.

The chain of 17 vertices is the worst case for squaring relative to its size: the path 0 → 16 has 16 edges, so it needs 24 = 16 and 4 changing squarings plus one confirming, 5 in total; the closure is the upper triangle including the diagonal. The two-cycle plus isolated vertex converges after 1 squaring (nothing changes: I ∨ A is already closed), and the isolated vertex 2 has only its own diagonal entry, which is why it must be present in the vertex list.

5. Mutually Reachable Groups (SCCs)

Vertices i and j are put in the same group when both R[i][j] and R[j][i] are true. Each group was compared with NetworkX strongly_connected_components.

Home and Exit are single-vertex groups: Home has no incoming edges and Exit has no outgoing edges. The closed pair Partner A ⇄ Partner B is a trap: once a walker enters it, it cannot leave, which matters for T2 and T3. In all four cluster graphs the closure gives exactly four groups of n/4 vertices, matching the four generator blocks; the links between blocks are one-way, so the closure is block upper-triangular:

6. Timing on cluster_graph(n, seed=8)

Each method was run three times on each size and the median is reported. Only the closure computation is timed: loading the JSON, building the graph, checking and plotting are outside the timer. The rule "after a run exceeds 5 s, skip that size and all larger ones for that method" was implemented, but it never triggered: the slowest Rust run took 0.89 s. The NumPy rows come from hw8_check.py on the same machine and are given only as a reference.

Squaring, bit rows0.177 ms (5 sq.)0.738 ms (5 sq.)1.665 ms (5 sq.)5.067 ms (5 sq.)
Squaring, scalar bool7.242 ms (5 sq.)17.324 ms (5 sq.)121.446 ms (5 sq.)892.640 ms (5 sq.)
NumPy Warshall (np.outer, reference)4.763 ms15.450 ms43.948 ms151.866 ms
NumPy int64 R @ R, threshold (reference)6.137 ms (5 sq.)126.632 ms (5 sq.)2160.367 ms (5 sq.)9493.185 ms (5 sq.)

What is vectorised

  • Bit rows (Rust): a row is stored as ⌈n/64⌉ u64 words, and "row i OR row k" is done word by word, so one machine instruction handles 64 matrix entries (word-level parallelism). In the Boolean product the same row-OR is used for every k with R[i][k] true. These simple loops can additionally be auto-vectorised by the compiler, but I did not rely on it.
  • Scalar bool (Rust): one entry per operation. Squaring uses the textbook i, j, k loops with an early exit as soon as one k is found.
  • NumPy reference: Warshall loops over k in Python, but each step R |= np.outer(R[:, k], R[k]) is one vectorised C operation on all n² entries. The squaring uses R @ R on int64 and then > 0; NumPy's integer matrix product does not go to BLAS, so it is a slow C loop: 9493.185 ms at n = 512.

Fewer matrix operations does not mean less work

Repeated squaring needs only 5 "matrix operations" here, while Warshall needs n = 512 update rounds. But one Boolean product costs Θ(n³) (n² entries, each an OR over n terms), and a Warshall round costs only Θ(n²), so Warshall does about n³ work in total and squaring about 5·n³ (in general ⌈log₂(longest path)⌉ + 1 products). The measurements agree: at n = 512 squaring with bit rows is 2.6× slower than Warshall with bit rows, and the scalar versions differ by 8.9×. Warshall also skips every row i with R[i][k] false, and the data layout matters more than the operation count: bit rows make Warshall 52× faster than the scalar version with the same algorithm. The scalar times grow by about 7–8× per doubling of n, as expected for n³. The bit-row times grow by only about 4× here, because with n ≤ 512 a row is at most 8 words, so the n/64 factor is still small next to the per-row overhead.

Task T2: Walkers versus a probability vector

0. Transition Matrix

P is built from the base mini-web by dividing each row of weights by its row sum, so P[i][j] = w(i → j) / Σk w(i → k). Exit (node 11) has no outgoing edges, so its row is set explicitly to 1/12 for every vertex: a walker standing on Exit jumps to a uniformly random vertex (possibly Exit itself). This is a rule for the dangling row only; every other row follows its links. For the comparison rule, "uniform among outgoing neighbours", every outgoing edge of a vertex gets the same probability and the Exit row stays the same. Both matrices are built in Rust (transition in src/lib.rs); every row sums to 1 and has no negative entries.

1. Simulator and Exact Vector

  • Simulation (Sampler in src/lib.rs, src/bin/T2.rs): each of the M walkers starts at 0 Home and makes exactly t transitions. A transition draws u uniformly from [0, 1) (SplitMix64) and takes the first destination whose cumulative row probability exceeds u. Only the final position of each walker is counted, not the vertices it visited on the way, and the counts are divided by M. Every walker is independent; every (rule, t, M) uses its own recorded seed.
  • Prediction: p0 = (1, 0, …, 0) for Home, and pt+1 = pt P (row vector times matrix), repeated t times. No matrix power is formed.
  • Error: L1 = Σv |empirical(v) − pt(v)|, which is between 0 and 2.

3. Comparison at t = 10

Both graphs use the same colour scale (0 to 0.33), so equal colours mean equal probabilities.

Which vertices gain or lose probability under weighted transitions?

  • Gain: Projects (+0.065), Research (+0.036), the course group 1–4 (together +0.084) and Updates. The heavy edges keep walkers inside the two groups: Home → Courses has weight 3 (3/4 instead of 1/2), so more walkers start in the course group, which can only be left through Graphs → Research; and Research → Projects has weight 4 (0.8 instead of 0.5), and from Projects about 61% of walkers are back at Research within two steps (1/3 directly, 1/6 via People, 1/9 via Updates).
  • Lose: Partner B (−0.167), Partner A (−0.042) and slightly People. Under the uniform rule Research sends half its walkers to People, and People sends half of those straight into Partner A, so the trap is reached faster: after 10 steps it holds 60.5% of the probability with the uniform rule but only 39.6% with weights.
  • Inside the trap the walkers alternate 9 → 10 → 9 every step. The split between Partner A and Partner B at t = 10 therefore depends on the parity of the step at which a walker entered (always at Partner A), so the two values are not equal and would swap roles at odd and even t.
  • Home keeps almost nothing (only walkers that jumped from Exit back to Home), and Exit stays small because it is reached only through Updates and is left immediately.

4. Does Increasing M Help?

To answer this without relying on one lucky or unlucky run, each (t, M) was repeated with 40 further seeds for M = 100, 300, 1,000, 3,000, 10,000, 30,000.

On average, yes: the error falls like 1/√M, so 10 times more walkers give about √10 ≈ 3.2 times smaller L1 (for t = 10 the mean goes from 0.0795 at M = 1,000 to 0.0245 at M = 10,000). But it is a statement about the average, not about every run. With the same seed index, M = 10,000 was better than M = 1,000 in 40/40 cases for t = 10 and 40/40 for t = 3, but only in 33/40 cases for t = 1. At t = 1 there are only two outcomes (Courses or Research), so the error is just 2·|share at Courses − 0.75| and a small sample can hit the 75 : 25 split exactly (the points on the bottom edge of the plot are runs with L1 = 0). Larger t spreads the probability over more vertices, so the L1 sum collects more small errors and is larger for the same M.

Task T3: Teleportation and PageRank

0. Model

The same weighted P as in T2 is used, with the uniform Exit row. Teleportation is applied as a vector update, without building any all-to-all matrix:

pk+1 = (1 − rho) · pk P + rho / n · (1, …, 1)

Since pk sums to 1, this is exactly "with probability rho jump to a uniformly random page, otherwise follow P". The start is p0 = all mass at Partner A (node 9). For rho > 0 the iteration stops when ||pk+1 − pk||1 < 10−10, or after 2,000 iterations (then it would be reported as not converged). Code: teleport_step, pagerank and long_walk in src/lib.rs, experiment src/bin/T3.rs.

1. rho = 0: Trapping and Oscillation

0 Home1 Courses2 Algorithms3 Trees4 Graphs5 Research6 Projects7 People8 Updates9 Partner A10 Partner B11 Exit
p0000000000100
p1000000000010
p2000000000100
p3000000000010
p4000000000100
p5000000000010

The six distributions p0 … p5 alternate between "everything at Partner A" and "everything at Partner B". Partner A has a single link to Partner B and Partner B a single link back, and T1 showed that {9, 10} is a closed SCC: nothing leaves it. So without teleportation

  • trapping: once mass is in {9, 10} it stays there forever (from any start, all mass would end up here, apart from mass still on its way);
  • oscillation: the cycle has period 2, so pk never settles. Every step changes the vector by L1 = 2. After 2,000 iterations the change is still 2: the iteration has not converged, and the final iterate (all mass at Partner A, because 2,000 is even) is not a stationary distribution. A stationary vector does exist (½ on each of 9 and 10), but power iteration from this start never reaches it.

All three positive values converge. The change shrinks by a factor of exactly (1 − rho) per step: the 2-cycle gives P an eigenvalue −1, which the teleportation step scales to −(1 − rho), and this is the slowest part to die out. That is why the iteration counts are almost exactly log(10−10/2) / log(1 − rho) (the grey numbers), and why rho = 0.05 needs about four times as many steps as rho = 0.20.

Effect of teleportation

  • It makes the chain escape the trap: from 9 and 10 a walker leaves with probability rho · 10/12 per step. The trap mass falls from 0.681 (rho = 0.05) to 0.521 and 0.368.
  • It removes the oscillation: some mass is always spread uniformly, so the period-2 behaviour is damped and there is a single stationary vector, the same for every start.
  • Larger rho makes the vector flatter (closer to 1/12 everywhere) and converge faster, but it also tells less about the links. Home stays lowest: no page links to it, so it only receives teleportation mass (rho/12) and the 1/12 share of the Exit row.
  • Partner A is above Partner B for every rho: Partner B is linked only from Partner A (π10 = rho/12 + (1 − rho)(π9 + π11/12)), while Partner A is also linked from People and Updates.

5. Checks

  • All vectors are nonnegative and sum to 1 (check_distribution).
  • For rho = 0.05, 0.10, 0.20 on the mini-web and rho = 0.10 on clusters_256, check_pagerank (NetworkX with alpha = 1 − rho and uniform dangling rule) agrees within 10−8.
  • rho = 0 is not passed to the checker (it requires positive rho, and the iteration does not converge).

PageRank is not a universal measure of importance. Here the two partner pages rank highest only because they form a closed loop that keeps the walker; "Home", which every user would call the most important page, ranks lowest because nothing links to it. Changing rho, the weights, the dangling rule or one link (see web_escape) changes the ranking.

Task T4: A small flow problem: undoing a choice

0. Network

s → A, s → B (each student can be assigned once), A → X, A → Y, B → X (availability), X → t, Y → t (one seat each). Every capacity is 1, so a flow of value k is an assignment of k students. The trace below was done by hand first; the Rust program (src/bin/T4.rs, residual network FlowNet in src/lib.rs) then replays exactly these two paths, draws every step and confirms that no other choice was possible.

1. Hand Trace

  1. Augmentation 1: s → A → X → t, bottleneck 1 (panel 1 → 2). Student A takes session X. Value 1.
  2. Residual network after it (panel 3). For every original edge u → v with flow f and capacity c the residual network has u → v with c − f (if positive) and a reverse edge v → u with f (if positive). The used edges s → A, A → X, X → t are replaced by A → s, X → A, t → X. What remains forward: s → B, B → X, A → Y, Y → t.
  3. Augmentation 2: from s only B is reachable, from B only X, and from X only the reverse edge X → A; then A → Y → t. The unique augmenting path is s → B → X → A → Y → t, bottleneck 1 (the program enumerated all simple s–t paths in this residual network and found only this one). Value 2.
  4. Final residual network (panel 5): s has no outgoing residual edge, so t is unreachable and the flow is maximum.

What the reverse edge means

Traversing X → A cancels one unit of flow on A → X. In terms of people: B wants X, but X is taken by A; the path tells A to give up X and move to Y, which is free. The first decision (A in X) was not wrong forever, it is undone. Without reverse edges a greedy method would stop after the first path at value 1, with B unassigned.

2. Final Allocation and Certificate

Original edgeCapacityFlow
A → X10
A → Y11
B → X11
X → t11
Y → t11
s → A11
s → B11

Final assignment: A → Y, B → X, both students placed, flow value 2. The source side found by residual reachability is S = {s}; the cut edges are s -> A, s -> B, total capacity 2.

Why this proves optimality: every unit of flow from s to t has to cross from S to the other side through some cut edge, so any flow has value ≤ the capacity of any cut. We have a flow of value 2 and a cut of capacity 2, so no flow can be larger, and no cut can be smaller. (Here it is also obvious: only two students exist.) Checking all 16 cuts that separate s from t shows that the minimum capacity 2 is reached by five of them: {s}, {s, B}, {s, B, X}, {s, A, B, X}, {s, A, B, X, Y}.

3. Code Check with the Course Helpers

The hand flow and source side were passed to check_flow: capacities, conservation and flow value = cut capacity = 2 all hold. NetworkX maximum_flow as a second check also gives value 2 (and here even the same edge flows). The figures below are drawn by the notebook helpers draw_flow (with the cut) and draw_residual:

4. Interactive Trace
